planting.note: Plant container-grown trees or rooted cuttings in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Eureka is an old American pomegranate cultivar noted for compact size and reliable production of small, deep-red, tart-sweet fruit. Self-fertile; no cross-pollination needed.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate a wide range of soil types including clay and alkaline soils. Eureka is a long-cultivated American pomegranate valued for its compact, more shrubby growth habit compared to larger cultivars, making it a good fit for smaller yards or container culture, and for producing small to medium, bright red fruit with tender, tart-sweet, deep-red arils over a long harvest season. Its attractive orange-red spring flowers also make it useful as a flowering ornamental in addition to fruit production. Trees are drought-tolerant once established; prune lightly after the first year to encourage branching and fruit spur development, since pomegranates fruit on new wood.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pomegranates for Texas

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees or rooted cuttings in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Al-Sirin-Nar is a Turkish pomegranate cultivar prized for large fruit with deep-red, soft-seeded arils and rich, sweet-tart flavor. Self-fertile; no cross-pollination needed.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate a wide range of soil types including clay and alkaline soils. Al-Sirin-Nar, a Turkish cultivar whose name translates roughly to 'sweet pomegranate,' bears large fruit filled with deep-red, notably soft-seeded arils and a rich, well-balanced sweet-tart flavor that has made it one of the more sought-after fresh-eating pomegranate cultivars among collectors. Trees are vigorous and productive, ripening fruit in the fall for fresh eating, juicing, or preserving. Trees are drought-tolerant once established; prune lightly after the first year to encourage branching and fruit spur development, since pomegranates fruit on new wood.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees or rooted cuttings in spring; in zone 9 plant February-April. Kazake is a cold-hardy Central Asian pomegranate cultivar noted for tolerating colder winter temperatures than many fruiting pomegranates. Self-fertile; no cross-pollination needed.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; pomegranates tolerate a wide range of soil types including clay and alkaline soils. Kazake, originating from the cold-winter regions of Central Asia, is grown chiefly for its exceptional cold hardiness among fruiting pomegranate cultivars, tolerating winter temperatures that would damage or kill less hardy selections, which gives extra insurance against rare hard freezes in zone 8b-9a gardens. Fruit is medium-sized with dark red skin and tart-sweet, deep-red arils, ripening in fall for fresh eating and juicing. Trees are drought-tolerant once established and long-lived; prune lightly after the first year to encourage branching and fruit spur development, since pomegranates fruit on new wood.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in spring; Meader is a cold-hardy American persimmon cultivar bred by Elwyn Meader at the University of New Hampshire, notable for being self-fertile without needing a pollinizer.

directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; American persimmon is notably drought-tolerant when established and thrives without supplemental fertilization in most soils. Meader, bred by plant breeder Elwyn Meader at the University of New Hampshire, is prized among American persimmon cultivars for being reliably self-fertile, setting a good crop of medium, orange, sweet fruit without needing a separate pollinizer tree, unlike many native persimmon seedlings that require both a male and female tree. Its far-northern breeding origin also gives it excellent cold hardiness well beyond what most fruiting persimmons need in the Gulf South. Fruit ripens after fall frost, becoming sweet and non-astringent only once fully soft.
sources: University of New Hampshire Cooperative Extension

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in spring; Prok is a large-fruited American persimmon cultivar selected for size well above typical wild seedling persimmons, with rich, sweet flavor once fully ripe.

directions: Plant in full sun in any well-drained soil; American persimmon is notably drought-tolerant when established and thrives without supplemental fertilization in most soils. Prok bears notably large fruit for an American persimmon selection, several times the size of typical wild seedling fruit, with rich, sweet, honeyed flavor once fully soft and ripe after fall frost. Its large fruit size makes it a favorite among American persimmon collectors seeking improved selections closer in scale to Asian persimmon cultivars while retaining the superior cold hardiness of the native species. As with other American persimmons, fruit remains astringent and inedible until fully soft-ripe, so avoid picking before that stage.
